newsitem.title: INDIA: India markets seen falling on traders' dashed hopes.
newsitem.headline: India markets seen falling on traders' dashed hopes.

text.p: Indian brokers foresaw heavy blood-letting when Indian stock markets opened on Friday after the government failed to deliver new economic measures traders had built their hopes on.
Moves by the country's market watchdog to open the country's debt market to foreign investors partly softened the blow, but traders said the markets had no place to go but down.
"It's a total let-down," said Paresh Khandwala, director of Khandwala Finances Ltd, a brokerage firm that trades mainly on India's National Stock Exchange.
"You'll see a good dip tomorrow -- 100-150 points fall."
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark share index surged 24 percent in the New Year on dealers' hopes of a reform package before profit-taking took the steam out of the rally.
The top-30 Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index closed Thursday at 3,510.05 -- off the January 16 intraday peak of 3,812.31 and compared to 1996 close of 3,085.20.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda had promised on Monday to unveil the new package before he departed for the World Economic Forum summit at Davos in Switzerland on January 31.
But traders' hopes crashed to earth after Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told newsmen on Thursday that a string of measures announced during January had constituted the package.
"Taken together, I believe, they constitute a cohesive package of decisions which will impart greater thrust to economic reforms," Chidambaram said.

Anticipation had built up to a feverish pitch after Deve Gowda told a group of industrialists last month that his government was working on a package to revive India's capital markets, gripped in a three-year bear hug.
Khandwala said the government should not tinker with the market by raising false hopes.
"How can a government do this? The PM says one thing... the finance minister says something else."

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) announced a move to open up the government debt market to foreigners, along with a swathe of new rules governing share dealings, including fresh regulations related to takeovers.

"The SEBI announcement about foreign institutional investors (FIIs) being allowed to invest in the debt market is an excellent decision," Vijay Pandya, chief dealer at Classic Share and Stock Brokers, told Reuters.
The market monitor also announced measures to streamline corporate takeover procedures.
It also said it had approved a stock lending scheme, whereby shareowners can lend their shares for a limited period to a third party who will trade them.
"Stock lending will bring more liquidity into the markets," Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds' Securities, said.
Traders said they could only hope for steps to revive India's flagging economy when Chidambaram presents his budget for 1997/98 (April-March) to parliament on February 28.
"Now the budget has to be good," said a trader at a European brokerage. "There can be nothing worse than this."
Some steps to perk up the economy are essential if the government is to meet its projected target of 6.8 percent growth in GDP in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March).
But traders still smarting from the letdown were unwilling to look for any silver linings.
"Typically, markets tend to rise only if expectations are more than met. It is the same here," said Prashant Purker, head of sales at Peregrine Capital.
